sections.heading: Install the embedded SDK
sections.text: Dependabot for agents. At runtime. Detect API drift as agents run, apply reviewed and verified runtime repairs, and turn drift evidence into validated source fixes and draft pull requests. Pre-alpha. Detection requires configured windows. Runtime repair is opt-in for supported changes. Source-fix tooling is available locally; hosted PR automation is not yet qualified. Install the pre-alpha Node or Python SDK with `npm install agindow@0.1.0-alpha.3` or `pip install agindow==0.1.0a2`. Your application still needs any credentials required by the vendor API; keep them in its existing client or configuration. The embedded AGINDOW SDK does not require a separate AGINDOW API key, dashboard login or hosted endpoint. After installation, select and configure a detector. The statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect. Statistical detection also requires representative baseline and current-traffic windows.

sections.heading: Use the integration that fits your application
sections.text: Most applications should use the embedded SDK in the process that already calls the vendor API. The local guard HTTP host and read-only MCP evidence surface are optional advanced boundaries, not mandatory steps for embedded SDK users.

sections.heading: From call to evidence
sections.text: Wrap the callable, inspect a size-limited copy of its request and response, decide under the mode fixed for that call, and send the audit record only to a destination you configured. A mode (observe, repair, or strict) is configuration. A decision (ok, repaired, degraded, bypassed, or blocked) describes what one call produced.

sections.heading: Build understanding in the right order
sections.text: AGINDOW compares configured evidence for API calls made by agents. A vendor may still return valid JSON while a field’s meaning, values or completeness have changed. Evaluate current capabilities, then use Quickstart to wrap one API call. Configure detection with the complete example in Detection and evidence windows. Learn outcome handling and the reference for your chosen boundary next. Selective repair is off by default and requires explicit reviewed rules and independent verification. A finding, candidate patch or audit artifact does not independently prove persisted write correctness.

sections.heading: Start with an embedded SDK
sections.text: For most applications, use the Node or Python SDK in the process that already calls the vendor API. Keep the vendor credentials that application already requires in its existing client or configuration. The embedded AGINDOW SDK needs no separate AGINDOW API key, dashboard session or HTTP endpoint. Quickstart connects one API read. Detection is a separate setup step: the statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect.

sections.heading: Availability and safety
sections.text: Embedded SDKs are published pre-alpha packages. AGINDOW does not currently operate hosted guard or MCP endpoints. The statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect. Selective repair is off by default; reviewed rename rules and independent verification enable it. Do not rely on a finding, successful installation or simulation as evidence that production writes are protected.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text: Install the SDK, observe an API call, inspect the result, and learn how to enable verified repair. AGINDOW runs inside your application around a call you already own. It can detect configured drift signals and apply eligible repairs when explicitly configured. Allow about five minutes with Node 22.6+ (for the TypeScript run command) or Python 3.11+, a working project (and Python virtual environment), and an existing read-only endpoint that returns JSON. This first pass connects the SDK; it does not yet configure drift detection. You need no separate AGINDOW API key, account or hosted service.

sections.heading: 1. Install the SDK
sections.text: Choose one language. In your project directory, run `npm install agindow@0.1.0-alpha.3` for Node, or `pip install agindow==0.1.0a2` in your Python environment. Packages include the engine; no Rust build or extra HTTP library is required. The version notice above tells you whether this pair is published or still prepared for release.

sections.heading: 2. Wrap one API call
sections.text: Choose the TypeScript or Python tab below. Save it as `quickstart.mts` or `quickstart.py`. The sample makes one JSON GET to `API_URL` using the standard HTTP client. For an API that needs authentication, keep its headers and credentials in your existing client and replace only the `readApi` / `read_api` function. `sdk.guard` wraps the function; the call returns your API result. Start in `observe`: it reports configured findings without changing the payload or blocking the call. Use a read you can safely run once.

sections.heading: 3. Run and inspect
sections.text: Set `API_URL` in your terminal to your working HTTPS JSON endpoint. Then run `node --experimental-strip-types quickstart.mts` or `python quickstart.py`. Your normal vendor credentials are still required if the endpoint needs them. Expect your API response followed by `AGINDOW events: []` when the engine loads and no detector or repair rule is selected. `sdk.recent()` contains recent local events; the listener prints findings when detection is configured. An empty event list does not prove there was no drift.

# Replace this with your existing read-only JSON endpoint.
export API_URL="https://your-api.example/read-only-endpoint"
# Run ONE command for the language you saved:
node --experimental-strip-types quickstart.mts
# or: python quickstart.py

The original API call failed. Check the URL, vendor authorization and response before adding detection.

sections.heading: 4. Configure drift detection
sections.text: The statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect. Wrapping a call does not automatically learn its baseline. Supply representative baseline and current-traffic JSON windows for the same operation, select the fields to compare, and create the SDK with that `selection`. A configured drift finding appears in the `drift` listener and `sdk.recent()`. Keep observe mode while you evaluate the evidence. The detection guide contains the complete runnable example and explains how to replace its demonstration data with your own windows.

links.label: Set up detection and run its complete example

sections.heading: 5. Enable verified repair when ready
sections.text: Selective repair is off by default. For a supported top-level field rename, configure reviewed migration rules and an independent synchronous verifier with `selectiveRepair` in Node or `selective_repair` in Python. Start with those rules in observe mode, then choose `repair` only after verifying them against your application. Changing the mode alone does not create a repair rule. A `drift` event reports a finding; a `repair` event means an accepted patch was applied. `strict` can halt unresolved drift; it is not a shortcut to setup. Automatic source fixes and hosted draft PR creation are not enabled by this integration.

import json
import os
from urllib.request import urlopen
from agindow import Agindow

sdk = Agindow(mode="observe")
sdk.on("drift", lambda event: print("Drift:", event.verdict))

def read_api(url: str) -> object:
    with urlopen(url, timeout=10) as response:
        result: object = json.load(response)
        return result

read = sdk.guard(read_api, tool="vendor.read", operation="read")
try:
    result = read(os.environ["API_URL"])
    print("API result:", result)
    print("AGINDOW events:", [event.type for event in sdk.recent()])
finally:
    sdk.close()

sections.heading: What the skill covers
sections.text: Node and Python setup, explicit detector selection, call semantics, findings and error handling, safe write idempotency, audit delivery with explicit queue limits, and read-only MCP evidence. The statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect. Selective repair is off by default and can be enabled with reviewed rules and independent verification. Installing a skill does not configure detection, change live traffic or enable a hosted service.

sections.heading: Compare real API responses before installation
sections.text: The /try page collects actual GET responses from an HTTPS JSON API you choose. Compare HTTP status checks, a response JSON Schema you supply and AGINDOW statistical detection on the same current window. No sample scenario, injected change, generated finding or fabricated write receipt is provided. The browser guest is the same WASM artifact used by the SDKs.

sections.heading: 1. Choose a read-only API and field
sections.text: Enter an HTTPS endpoint you own or have permission to test, and choose a populated response field using a JSON Pointer such as /amount. Optional API headers are sent directly to that endpoint. Browser cookies are omitted and redirects are refused. CORS must permit this website and the selected headers; if it does not, run SDK evaluation in the application that already owns the API client. There is no AGINDOW proxy or credential discovery.

sections.heading: 2. Capture a baseline
sections.text: Choose Capture baseline. Collection makes 128 real GET requests at most one per second, normally taking about two minutes. A progress count and Stop control remain visible. Each complete JSON response is limited to 32 KiB and each request has a ten-second timeout. Non-JSON, oversized and incomplete collection are errors, never padded with generated data. HTTP failure statuses remain visible; 429 stops collection. Collection starts are rate-limited to three per ten minutes per client and thirty per instance, using short-lived address digests. Each window has a five-minute overall deadline. This process-local limit is not a global quota on your API; provider limits still apply. Use a read endpoint where repeated requests are appropriate and respect its limits and charges.

sections.heading: 3. Capture current responses
sections.text: Later choose Capture current for the same URL and headers. Both windows must share the same request scope. Choose comparable calls: different users, filters, seasons or normal business traffic can change distributions without an API migration. The tool does not introduce drift to force a finding. Capture before and after an actual change you are investigating; an unchanged service can legitimately produce no findings.

sections.heading: 4. Select a schema comparison
sections.text: Optionally paste a self-contained response JSON Schema, such as the response schema from an OpenAPI 3.1 contract. Local references are supported; remote references and extracting a schema from a complete OpenAPI document are not. Without a schema, the result is Not compared, never an implied pass. Constraints such as numeric limits can catch semantic differences too. The page evaluates these selected checks, not every contract suite, observability product or possible invariant.

sections.heading: 5. Read the side-by-side evidence
sections.text: Choose Compare after both captures finish. HTTP checks report the actual status counts. Schema checks report how many current bodies satisfy your constraints. AGINDOW evaluates the selected response field using the real guest and reports findings, classification and eligible detectors. Bypass or no eligible detector is unavailable evidence, not a clean result. If status/schema pass while AGINDOW finds drift, that is the result for these windows and these checks, not a universal comparison claim. No finding is a valid outcome.

sections.heading: 6. Inspect and clear your data
sections.text: Inspect captured responses shows the latest three complete bodies from each window with timestamps and statuses. Data and headers remain in tab memory, are not persisted by the app, and are cleared on reload or Clear responses and headers. Copy comparison summary excludes headers, query strings and raw bodies. This flow reads APIs in observe mode; it does not execute writes, apply repairs or prove persisted write correctness.

sections.heading: Authenticated Test workflow
sections.text: Use Review authenticated Test workflow on /try to sign in, choose an authorized workspace and load host-reviewed non-production operation profiles. Review the operation, exact committed JS/TS repository/base, capture limits, deadline, retention and service availability before confirming runtime execution consent. The browser cannot submit an API URL, executable code, verifier commands or repository binding to this private API. Viewing a page starts no capture, generation or publication. Execution requires an owner, recent authentication and fresh server authority; viewers can inspect admitted evidence only.

sections.heading: Trace each promised outcome
sections.text: A retained Test run links baseline/current capture and findings to the packaged SDK runtime receipt, original input, selective rename patch, independent verifier decision and actual upstream outcome. The source step shows its minimal diff, exact base/patch/fact references, unrelated-context preservation and confined before-fail/after-pass validation. A fresh standing deterministic source/publication grant is managed in the finding’s existing source-fix controls, separately from runtime consent. Successful matching validation can trigger a draft without another per-run PR confirmation. A proposed repair, observe/bypass decision, inconclusive validation, exported patch or PR preview never establishes all three outcomes. Provider draft creation, current PR lifecycle, CI, merge, deployment and observed resolution remain separate.

sections.heading: Unavailable services and retained evidence
sections.text: The default deployment has no Test execution host, validation runner or publisher. Full-flow execution remains unavailable until the workspace owner configures the bounded execution services and records a qualified isolated run with actual API, independent validation and real provider receipts. Local injected test receipts are labelled Local test evidence. Stable or insufficient windows may legitimately abstain. Refresh durable run status to read completed evidence; retained data is marked stale on an outage. Auth refusal clears the private view. Cancel future run steps requests a host fence; it cannot undo completed writes. Never retry an uncertain vendor write. Response inspection cannot prove persisted business correctness. Source/publisher outages do not add a guard dependency.

sections.heading: Inspect source separately
sections.text: The second workspace scans your supplied TypeScript/JavaScript source for tool definitions and wrapper hints. Source stays local. These hints do not establish an active runtime guard. The editor starts empty; results come only from the code you supply. The Python tab highlights your own source, without Python static analysis or IntelliSense. This scan does not call APIs; choose Detect drift to collect real API responses. No source code is executed.

sections.heading: Wrap → inspect → decision → audit → feedback
sections.text: Wrap the callable. Inspect a complete request and response up to the configured size limit before dispatch and after a response. Supplied OpenAPI, schema or contract evidence and runtime failures are inputs; they are not themselves detection. Fix the mode for both phases. Produce ok / repaired / degraded / bypassed / blocked. Send the audit record only to a destination you configured. Optional feedback informs later investigation; it cannot authorize replay or change a completed decision. Response inspection cannot undo a completed upstream write; availability faults bypass inspection even for writes.

sections.heading: Evidence classes
sections.text: A finding describes drift evidence. A patch describes a proposed or verified selective change. An incident is a separately admitted accounting unit. A candidate is not an applied repair; an audit artifact is not automatically write-integrity proof. Incomplete captures are unavailable evidence, not malformed vendor bodies.

sections.heading: Trusted rename source versus inferred meaning
sections.text: A fictional mechanical rename (for example order_ref → order_id) may be considered only when a trusted migration source confirms the rename, an independent check verifies the constraint, confidence is sufficient and untouched caller fields are preserved. Schema acceptance and confidence alone are insufficient to establish intent or persisted write correctness. An ambiguous source ↔ payment_method mapping cannot establish intended meaning from matching names or types; it is not a verified real payment-provider migration. Observe records without changing the call; repair mode blocks unresolved semantic write drift. Human review must be connected by the host application, and a review receipt does not execute or replay the write.

sections.heading: Byte identity
sections.text: No-repair paths preserve original payload identity. Selective repair changes only verified drifted fields and records byte_identical: false. Numeric coercion is not a repair. Selective repair is off by default; explicit reviewed rename rules and independent verification enable it.

sections.heading: Availability gate
sections.text: Infrastructure fault → transparent bypass, loudly, once per call. Warming, engine faults and unavailable inspection preserve original results and exceptions in every mode. Internal faults never become policy refusals. A bypass event is emitted once per call, not once per phase.

sections.heading: Policy is separate
sections.text: Known policy rejection remains a rejection: blocked is distinct from bypassed. Reads with incomplete policy repair can be degraded; strict is an explicit policy escalation. sections.heading: Uncertain or completed writes
sections.text: Inspect a retained completed outcome before deciding what to do next. Do not blindly replay a write with an uncertain outcome. Local replay state is not durable or distributed. Use the same upstream-enforced idempotency key in a remote request and its fallback; never generate a fresh key to repeat an uncertain write.

import json
from agindow import Agindow, Event

# Labelled local fixture: numeric magnitude shift, not live vendor traffic.
def selection_for(value: int, count: int = 128) -> dict[str, object]:
    return {
        "tenant": "demo", "connection": "local", "vendor": "synthetic",
        "operation": "demo.detect", "segment": "default",
        "fields": [{"side": "request", "path": "/value", "enumeration": True,
                    "baseline": [json.dumps({"value": 1}) for _ in range(count)],
                    "live": [json.dumps({"value": value}) for _ in range(count)]}],
    }


def observe(selection: dict[str, object] | None, value: int = 100) -> tuple[Event, ...]:
    sdk = Agindow(mode="observe", selection=selection)
    try:
        assert sdk.ready, sdk.load_error
        payload = {"value": value}

        @sdk.guard(tool="demo.detect", operation="read")
        def read(body: dict[str, int]) -> dict[str, int]:
            return body

        assert read(payload) is payload
        events = sdk.recent()
        assert not any(event.type in ("bypass", "repair", "blocked") for event in events)
        return events
    finally:
        sdk.close()


changed = observe(selection_for(100))
drift = next(event for event in changed if event.type == "drift")
verdict = drift.verdict
assert verdict is not None
assert verdict.findings == 1 and verdict.detectors == 5
assert verdict.drift_class == "semantic"
assert not verdict.bypassed and not verdict.halt and verdict.repair is None

assert not any(event.type == "drift" for event in observe(None))
assert not any(event.type == "drift" for event in observe(selection_for(100, 4)))

                  "detectors": verdict.detectors, "class": verdict.drift_class,

sections.heading: What API drift means
sections.text: API drift is a difference between the behavior your application expects and the behavior an API now exhibits. Shape drift changes fields or types. Semantic drift changes meaning or value patterns even when the payload still satisfies a schema. Unknown means the available evidence does not support a more specific classification. These classes are separate from detector names such as Unit.

sections.heading: What the statistical guest detects
sections.text: The embedded guest evaluates configured fields for numeric magnitude (Unit), enumeration, completeness, type and charset/format changes. Not every detector is eligible for every window. A finding says these configured windows differ under the detector’s rules; it does not establish a vendor migration’s intent or authorize repair. The demonstration’s Unit case uses 128 repeated synthetic documents per window to make the expected difference reproducible.

sections.heading: Choose comparable windows
sections.text: A baseline is the earlier reference window; live is the current comparison window. Supply arrays of complete raw JSON documents, not individual extracted numbers. Select independent calls for the same tenant, connection, vendor, operation and segment. Match request/response side and field path. Mixing currencies, customers or API operations can create differences unrelated to API drift. The fixed demonstration windows demonstrate configuration, not production calibration.

sections.heading: Configure the selection
sections.text: At SDK construction, selection supplies scope and fields. Each field has side (request or response), path, baseline, live and enumeration. Use a JSON Pointer such as /value for the selected field. The selection operation must match the guarded tool name. This selection is frozen for the engine instance; configure changes call policy, not the engine’s windows. Construct a new instance for a new reviewed selection. These SDKs do not automatically fetch baselines or refresh them from a dashboard.

sections.heading: Request and response inspection
sections.text: Request inspection occurs before the callable; response inspection follows its result or error. A request finding uses the configured request-side windows, and response findings use response-side evidence. Keep these datasets separate. A response halt can follow a completed vendor write and cannot undo it. Whole malformed bodies, truncated inspection copies and transport failures are different evidence conditions.

sections.heading: When no finding is inconclusive
sections.text: A default instance with no selection has no findings. Missing fields, ineligible detectors, insufficient samples, scope mismatch or exhausted inspection work can prevent a useful verdict. Different detector families have different eligibility requirements; 128 is the fixture window size, not a promise that every production dataset of that size is sufficient. The demonstration verifies that four samples do not produce its Unit finding. Check bypass and readiness separately before interpreting silence.

sections.text: After installing the pinned SDK, use Node 22.6+ for the native TypeScript command. Save the TypeScript tab as `detect.mts` and run `node --experimental-strip-types detect.mts`, or save the Python tab as `detect.py` and run `python detect.py`. No vendor credentials or network call is used. This labelled local magnitude shift compares baseline value 1 with current value 100 and verifies a Unit finding. Unchanged, unconfigured and insufficient-window controls must not claim detection. These fixed windows demonstrate detector setup, not production calibration or applied repair. Replace them only with independently collected comparable JSON windows for your selected operation.

A finding records configured evidence of a difference; it does not prove a safe repair or persisted write correctness.

Dashboard sessions, workload access tokens and vendor credentials have different purposes.

sections.heading: Audit delivery and retention

Queue overflow, restart and failed delivery can lose evidence. Recent events are a local rolling buffer, not an archive. The Python SDK does not expose the guest audit drain. Remote retrieval has separate process-local retention and access checks; missing evidence is not proof that a call did not execute.

sections.heading: Handle writes and remote trust
sections.text: Mark write operations explicitly. Reconcile uncertain outcomes before retrying, and require vendor-enforced idempotency for remote fallback. Use only a remote endpoint you intentionally configured; never infer an execution URL from the website. Verify signed OpenAPI against an independently trusted key, not a key supplied with the same untrusted response.

No hosted guard or uptime guarantee is available. Evaluate the configured boundary and data handling in your application before deciding whether this release meets your requirements.

sections.heading: 7. Configure Python RemoteAuth
sections.text: Install the pinned Python SDK and a host Ed25519 signing library. This optional example uses cryptography (install it in your workload environment); it is not an AGINDOW dependency. Save the helper as keyless_auth.py. Call connect_self_hosted with the same public handoff values and private_key_file. It prepares RemoteAuth with workload_identity and a separate ProofSigner, acquiring and refreshing outside guarded calls. The private key file remains customer-side. Close auth when finished; do not store a permanent assertion JWT.

from base64 import urlsafe_b64encode
from pathlib import Path
from time import time
from uuid import uuid4
import json
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey
from agindow import ProofSigner, RemoteAuth, workload_identity


def connect_self_hosted(*, exchange_endpoint: str, registration: str,
                        client_id: str, kid: str, audience: str,
                        private_key_file: str, tools: tuple[str, ...]) -> RemoteAuth:
    # This file is read only by the customer's workload, never uploaded.
    key = serialization.load_pem_private_key(Path(private_key_file).read_bytes(), password=None)
    if not isinstance(key, Ed25519PrivateKey):
        raise ValueError("Ed25519 client key required")

    def encode(value: object) -> str:
        return urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps(value, separators=(",", ":")).encode()).rstrip(b"=").decode()

    def assertion() -> str:
        now = int(time())
        header = encode({"alg": "EdDSA", "typ": "JWT", "kid": kid})
        claims = encode({"iss": client_id, "sub": client_id, "aud": audience,
                         "iat": now, "nbf": now, "exp": now + 120, "jti": str(uuid4())})
        value = header + "." + claims
        signature = urlsafe_b64encode(key.sign(value.encode())).rstrip(b"=").decode()
        return value + "." + signature

    proof_key = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
    public_x = urlsafe_b64encode(proof_key.public_key().public_bytes(
        serialization.Encoding.Raw, serialization.PublicFormat.Raw)).rstrip(b"=").decode()
    signer = ProofSigner(public_x, proof_key.sign)
    return RemoteAuth(workload_identity(exchange_endpoint=exchange_endpoint,
                      registration=registration, tools=tools, assertion=assertion), signer)

Neither retrying an old form nor the renewal job can resurrect a revoked grant. Already-issued tokens and stale leases retain bounded residual validity: conservatively up to 66 minutes under the documented host clock assumptions, not instant invalidation. Revoking the final grant stops the profile; ask the team running your deployment to review recovery before registering again.

sections.heading: Availability and prerequisites
sections.text: The prepared Node release includes local source binding and deterministic patch export commands. The wider source-fix workflow is an off-path local implementation under review. The default source, validation runner and draft publisher remain unconfigured; there is no managed source-fix service. The published SDK installation and quickstart do not enable this workflow. An integration owner must supply reviewed migration facts, an authorized repository and exact committed source binding, separate generation permission and an independently reviewed validation plan.

sections.heading: Generate a minimal candidate
sections.text: The deterministic recipe supports one explicitly bound top-level JavaScript or TypeScript request object key or direct response member access. It preserves local model names, comments and all unrelated bytes. Inventory hints are advisory and cannot select an edit. Export produces a patch and digest receipt without applying it, executing project code or opening a pull request. Generation alone leaves tests unvalidated. Ambiguous syntax, computed keys, collisions, dirty targets, stale commits or bindings, expired facts and mismatched scope refuse generation. Python source rewrites, nested or array migrations and general-purpose code changes are unsupported.

sections.heading: Validate independently
sections.text: A separately configured confined runner checks the exact base, patch and reviewed facts in a disposable checkout. Before applying the patch, the specific regression must fail for its intended assertion; after applying it, that regression must pass, together with the configured type, contract and existing checks. Independent preservation checks reject unrelated changes, including attempts to alter tests or validators. Missing runners, setup failures, skipped checks and inconclusive results are not passes. A successful local receipt does not prove provider acceptance or persisted business effects.

sections.heading: Review publication authority
sections.text: Review the exact diff, base commit, fact citations and independent test receipt before granting publication. Source access, inference and publication permissions are separate. Automatic draft PR publication starts off and requires explicit scoped standing permission for a qualified deterministic recipe, or exact per-candidate approval. Every model candidate requires human approval of that exact candidate, even when inference is authorized. Pause or revoke consent to stop new writes; an already dispatched provider request still needs outcome reconciliation. Local export grants no publication permission.

sections.heading: Track outcomes separately
sections.text: A configured publisher may create a bot-owned branch and draft pull request only after fresh authority and validation checks. It cannot automatically merge, deploy or overwrite human changes. Uncertain create outcomes require scoped reconciliation rather than a second create request. Recorded PR creation, current lifecycle, CI, deployment and observed drift resolution are separate states; unknown states stay unknown. Local synthetic evaluation and fault tests do not qualify a live repository installation or hosted automation.

sections.heading: Read the evidence class first
sections.text: API declarations describe a specification change; observed drift describes configured runtime evidence; independently verified repair describes an admitted transformation. None automatically establishes either of the others. Compare the exact SDK, adapter, operation, request or response side, configuration and capture limits before interpreting a coverage row. Broad API coverage or a supported parser does not mean every migration can be repaired.

sections.heading: Compare bounded OpenAPI declarations
sections.text: The local background comparator accepts explicitly selected OpenAPI 3.0.x and 3.1.x JSON pairs. It compares operations, parameters, request bodies, response statuses, headers, media types, inherited security, descriptions and deprecations. Findings retain source versions and before/after JSON Pointers. Request enum widening and response enum narrowing are compatible declarations; other unproved shape changes remain potentially breaking. A declaration cannot replace an observed contract, authorize repair or configure the SDK guard.

sections.heading: Supply sources outside calls
sections.text: Background acquisition requires a configured host with pinned public HTTPS sources, an authorized operation selection and source snapshot storage. No default scheduler, source feed or acquisition service is enabled. Snapshots retain raw-source digests, selected versions, retrieval time and expiry. Default bounds are 64 KiB per document, 8,192 parsed nodes, depth 32, 256 reference expansions, 1,024 findings, a five-second deadline and one-hour source expiry. Redirects, external or missing references, cycles, unknown dialects, version mismatches and exhausted budgets produce partial evidence rather than a no-change claim. YAML and remote references are unsupported.

sections.heading: Separate supported recipes from planned coverage
sections.text: The embedded Node and Python repair option supports explicitly reviewed top-level JSON field renames with independent local verification and complete bounded captures. Nested or bounded-array SDK renames, finite string maps, exact null exceptions, numeric unit or epoch scaling and broader HTTP envelope or nested JSON detection remain planned. GraphQL, webhooks, SSE, WebSocket, pagination workflows and gRPC remain unsupported. A native library seam, background specification finding or future catalog row cannot enable these in an installed SDK.

sections.heading: Interpret missing and synthetic evidence
sections.text: The shared catalog supplies the documentation and public/dashboard coverage projections. Scoped configured and observed states require an authorized selection and a fresh observation watermark. Missing, future or stale watermarks cannot establish coverage, and the default host supplies no scoped observations or total-traffic source. Synthetic scorecards and mutation controls test local safety and scoring rules; they do not measure live detector accuracy, vendor write correctness or production calibration. Hosted qualification remains unavailable.

pages.title: What is API drift? Detect schema and statistical changes

sections.heading: Define the changed boundary
sections.text: API drift is a change in an integration’s observed contract or behavior that can invalidate its client’s assumptions. A removed response field is shape drift. A numeric amount changing magnitude can be a statistical signal of semantic drift even while the response remains valid JSON. A change is breaking relative to the consuming application: adding an unused field may be harmless, while removing a field used to authorize a write may be consequential. Detection identifies evidence of a difference; it does not automatically supply a correct migration.

sections.heading: Compare declared shape with observed behavior
sections.text: A schema comparison can identify a missing required property or a changed type when a schema and a complete response are available. Statistical detection instead compares explicitly selected fields in comparable baseline and current windows. Those windows must represent the same operation, phase and cohort. Mixing currencies, endpoints or tenants can produce apparent drift that is really a change in the sample population. AGINDOW does not learn a trustworthy production baseline just because a client was wrapped.

links.label: How the guard inspects a call

sections.heading: Example: an amount changes magnitude
sections.text: The detection guide supplies a labelled baseline of numeric values around 1 and a current window around 100 to the packaged statistical guest. Its configured Unit detector produces a finding; unchanged and insufficient-window controls do not establish successful detection. This is a controlled engine example, not evidence that a real vendor changed from dollars to cents. A magnitude difference is evidence to investigate, rather than permission to divide customer amounts by 100. If values keep the same distribution while their business meaning changes, statistical evidence alone can miss the change.

example.code: {"baseline":{"amount":1},"current":{"amount":100},"interpretation":"Investigate magnitude; do not infer a conversion"}

sections.heading: Keep findings separate from protection
sections.text: Observe mode records available findings and preserves the original call. A healthy engine with zero findings may mean that no detector was selected, that a window was insufficient or that no actionable signal was present. Check readiness, selection, scope and bypass separately. Configuring repair mode does not create representative windows and does not enable selective repair. In an agent workflow, label the tool and operation explicitly so the intended boundary is the one inspected.

sections.heading: Investigate before choosing a migration
sections.text: Retain the permitted evidence with your application’s redaction and retention rules. Compare the vendor’s declared contract with independent application facts. A field rename may be eligible for a reviewed mechanical rule, while an ambiguous payment-method mapping needs a decision about meaning. Never fabricate a missing field or infer business correctness merely from a schema accepting the payload. Detection, a proposed patch and an applied verified repair are three distinct outcomes.

For SDK integration, use independently collected representative windows and preserve the original client’s timeout, credential and cancellation behavior.

pages.title: How verified selective API drift repair works

sections.heading: Repair a reviewed change, not a guessed meaning
sections.text: API drift repair adapts an eligible changed API boundary so an integration can continue under its reviewed contract. AGINDOW’s published Node.js and Python SDKs implement verified selective repair for explicitly reviewed mechanical top-level field renames. The feature is off by default. It is not an autonomous semantic migration system: the application supplies the migration facts, tool and phase scope, confidence and independent verification. A detector finding is evidence of a difference and does not automatically become an applicable rename rule.

sections.heading: Example: preserve a customer identity during a rename
sections.text: Suppose a reviewed CRM migration changes contact_name to display_name. Independent application data already binds customer-123 to Ada. A local verifier checks the reviewed migration identity, the unchanged customer ID and that both old and new name values agree with that authoritative snapshot. The complete configuration example implements this with a local fixture callable in both languages. It does not contact a vendor. A schema check alone would accept many plausible names; it cannot establish that Ada is the intended customer.

example.code: {"before":{"id":"customer-123","contact_name":"Ada"},"after":{"id":"customer-123","display_name":"Ada"}}

links.label: Runnable Node.js and Python repair configuration

sections.heading: Configure the rule and verifier explicitly
sections.text: Node uses selectiveRepair with rules and verify; Python uses selective_repair with SelectiveRepair and RenameRule. Node rule names are from and to; Python uses source and target. Both scope by tool and request or response side. Prepare authoritative evidence outside the call: the synchronous verifier must not wait for a database, network service or LLM. Begin in observe, which reports a matched rule without changing payloads. Only repair or strict mode permits applying an independently accepted patch.

sections.heading: Apply only after every gate accepts
sections.text: Repair requires confidence of at least 0.97; strict requires at least 0.99. These are policy thresholds, not measured production accuracy. Complete supported capture, an eligible reviewed rule and a true synchronous verification result are required. Existing statistical findings, halts, malformed results and bypass are not cleared to force a repair. Source absence preserves identity; destination collisions, insufficient confidence or refusal leave the payload unchanged under the applicable policy. Verifier faults or unavailable capture bypass inspection and preserve upstream behavior.

sections.heading: Preserve untouched fields and inspect the event
sections.text: Only the reviewed top-level key changes; unrelated values are preserved. The no-repair path returns the original value by reference, while repair creates a replacement and records changed bytes honestly. A repair event describes an applied repair; a candidate or finding alone does not. Recent local events are bounded memory, not a durable archive. Configure storage separately when evidence must survive a restart. Successful payload verification does not prove that a vendor persisted the intended write.

sections.heading: Know when automated repair is unsafe
sections.text: Nested or array migrations, numeric conversions, enum rewriting and automatic rule discovery are outside this SDK option. A source/payment_method mapping can require business meaning that matching types cannot prove. Do not increase confidence to bypass missing evidence. An unresolved semantic write blocks in repair mode; unresolved shape drift can pass through for upstream rejection. Strict halts unresolved drift including reads, while infrastructure faults still bypass. A response halt cannot undo a completed upstream write, and replay requires separate outcome reconciliation.

pages.title: Runtime protection for AI agent API calls and writes

sections.heading: Put policy at the call boundary you own
sections.text: Runtime protection evaluates an agent’s API call at the point where the application can inspect input, decide whether to dispatch and inspect the completed outcome. AGINDOW brings the Dependabot for agents idea to runtime: configured detection supplies findings, verified selective repair may adapt eligible reviewed changes, and the chosen mode controls the policy decision. This boundary does not guarantee correct business actions or replace application authorization, vendor idempotency, retries or credentials. The published SDKs are pre-alpha tools for local evaluation; no generally available hosted guard service is offered.

sections.heading: Label writes before inspecting them
sections.text: A generic callable cannot tell whether it mutates vendor state. Use operation: write in Node or operation="write" in Python for calls that create or change state. Use unknown when effects are uncertain. A read label is not a harmless default for a callable that transfers money or updates a customer. Begin in observe with controlled fixtures: observe never mutates or blocks the call, so it does not enforce write protection. Detection selection and selective repair remain separate configuration decisions.

sections.heading: Example: distinguish the two halt phases
sections.text: Before dispatch, a request-phase policy halt can refuse the upstream operation. After the upstream has returned, a response-phase halt can report unresolved drift and retain available outcome evidence, but it cannot reverse the write. Consider an order-creation API returning an unexpected amount: inspect dispatch status and the retained response before deciding to send another order. An error reaching the agent is not evidence that the vendor created nothing.

example.code: {"request_halt":"Upstream dispatch refused","response_halt":"Upstream may already have completed; reconcile outcome"}

sections.heading: Understand fail-open and fail-closed decisions
sections.text: Observe preserves outcomes. In repair mode, reads can continue degraded; unresolved shape writes can pass through when upstream will reject, while unresolved semantic writes fail closed because a valid-looking request could silently produce the wrong result. Strict halts unresolved drift including reads and requires at least 0.99 for eligible verified repairs. An internal engine fault bypasses inspection in every mode. These conditional rules depend on available evidence and do not turn strict into an unconditional availability or protection guarantee.

sections.heading: Reconcile uncertainty before a retry
sections.text: A timeout can happen after the vendor committed a write. Check vendor state and retained outcome evidence before replaying. Preserve the same vendor-enforced idempotency key for the same logical operation where supported; a fresh key can create another write. Review receipts, process-local replay caches and local audit events do not provide distributed exactly-once execution. A receipt records a decision, not permission to execute or replay an operation.

sections.heading: Evaluate protection separately from detection
sections.text: Test request refusal, response outcomes, untouched payload preservation, independent verifier refusal and internal-fault bypass as separate behaviors. Check whether your configured detectors have representative windows and whether the selected adapter can capture a complete supported body. The read-only playground can help inspect an API response but cannot demonstrate write protection. Keep detection evidence, applied repairs and vendor-persisted correctness distinct when presenting evaluation results.

pages.title: Add AGINDOW to an existing API client

sections.heading: Choose one call you own
sections.text: Start with a safe read already used by your agent. The integration flow is agent → tool or API client → AGINDOW guard boundary → vendor API. Your application owns credentials, retries, operation labels and the original client; AGINDOW inspects the configured boundary and reports findings. Keep framework-specific behavior in the original client.

sections.heading: Get the call working, then configure detection
sections.text: Follow Quickstart to wrap a working API read first. Confirm its original response and error handling before adding a detector. Then choose request or response fields and independently collected comparable baseline/current windows for that operation. The complete detection guide supplies a labelled demonstration; replace its demo.detect operation and tool together. Do not copy synthetic data into an application and describe it as live evidence.

sections.heading: Wrap the callable
sections.text: Node: create the configured instance, await sdk.ready, then pass the callable to sdk.guard with tool and operation: read. Python: construct Agindow with selection, check ready, then use sdk.guard as a decorator or wrap the callable directly. Preserve the receiver when calling existing client methods; a small closure around the existing method is often easiest to review. The SDK does not supply vendor credentials or automatically change your transport.

sections.heading: Check behavior and evidence separately
sections.text: Verify the original return value and upstream exceptions remain intact in observe mode. Inspect drift and bypass events separately. An unchanged result is expected in observe; it does not prove there was no drift. Exercise the application’s own timeout and cancellation paths before expanding the boundary. Streaming and framework batch coverage require separate evaluation.

sections.heading: Identify the operation before wrapping
sections.text: A write creates or changes vendor state. Explicitly use operation: write in Node or operation="write" in Python; use unknown if the callable’s effect is uncertain. Generic callables default to read and cannot infer your business semantics. Start with fixture evaluation in observe mode, which preserves writes and does not enforce policy blocks.

sections.heading: Separate a proposal from an applied repair
sections.text: Detection identifies a difference. A proposed patch suggests a change. A verified repair additionally passes independent gates before application. Selective repair is off by default. The Node and Python SDKs accept reviewed rename rules and an independent verifier as explicit construction options. Enable selectiveRepair/selective_repair with reviewed rules and independent verification; repair or strict permits applying accepted patches. Mode alone does not supply a rule. Repair integrations require a trusted migration source, verification and sufficient confidence; matching field names or accepting a schema is insufficient.

sections.heading: Distinguish the two halt phases
sections.text: A request-phase halt refuses dispatch. A response-phase halt follows upstream completion and retains an outcome where available. Inspect AgindowDriftError.phase, verdict, outcome and hint. Do not turn every policy error into a retry. A review receipt does not execute a write or release a previously used idempotency key.

sections.heading: Reconcile uncertain outcomes
sections.text: After a timeout, transport error or missing outcome, determine whether the vendor accepted the original operation before sending another write. For remote fallback, require vendor-enforced idempotency and preserve the same key for the same logical operation. Never generate a fresh key merely to retry an uncertain write. Process-local replay caches and audit records cannot provide distributed exactly-once execution.

sections.heading: Verification checklist
sections.text: Use a controlled fixture to verify operation labels, request refusal, response outcome inspection and internal-fault bypass independently. Bypass preserves the original call even in strict mode; strict is not an infrastructure availability guarantee. No currently published detection example proves persisted write correctness or production protection.

sections.heading: Choose your integration
sections.text: Most application developers start with the embedded Node or Python SDK. Use the reference groups below when you choose HTTP execution, workload authentication, read-only MCP evidence or machine-readable documentation.

sections.heading: Guard execution
sections.text: Execute a tool call with POST /v1/guard on your own host. Read the envelope fields, upstream response behavior, diagnostic headers, errors and safe recovery steps. Audit and retained-outcome reads belong to this execution interface.

sections.heading: Workload identity (optional)
sections.text: Exchange a workload identity with POST /v1/token when your execution host requires an admitted, sender-bound identity. This endpoint issues a scoped token; it does not execute tools, create an account or authenticate a dashboard browser session. Embedded SDK use does not require this exchange.

sections.heading: MCP evidence (read-only)
sections.text: Read evidence through MCP: contracts, drift history, audit records, coverage and simulated repair proposals. The tools never execute vendor writes. Read the tool inputs/results, then the transport details or runnable MCP example.

sections.heading: Machine documents
sections.text: Use the document endpoints for signed API descriptions, Markdown docs and agent guidance. SKILL.md is the public best-practices skill. Availability of other machine documents depends on your configured MCP service; no managed MCP origin is issued.

sections.heading: Execute a configured tool
sections.text: Send an explicit JSON execution envelope to your own guard host. Use http://SIDECAR_HOST:8789, replacing SIDECAR_HOST with your configured local sidecar hostname; a Unix socket is also supported. A configured connection selects the upstream tool and its credentials; callers cannot supply arbitrary upstream URLs or authorization headers. This is a separate execution host from the read-only MCP interface. Managed guard execution is not available.

sections.heading: Request fields
sections.text: Use Content-Type: application/json. Unknown top-level fields are rejected. Required fields have no implicit mode or operation default on HTTP.

rows: Configured tool name; 1–256 UTF-8 bytes, no control characters or slash.
Authorized connection handle; same identifier bounds as tool. Not a credential.
Must match the configured route. Treat unknown as a write for idempotency.
Upstream request arguments; at most 8 MiB of encoded JSON.
Policy for both inspection phases; observe does not mutate or block.
1–256 UTF-8 bytes, no controls; forwarded as Idempotency-Key. The upstream must enforce deduplication.
Defaults to {}. Does not grant authority or configure the detector.
A non-null value is rejected. No durability service is selected through this request.

sections.heading: Try a configured local read
sections.text: Requires a running sidecar with conn_example/vendor.read already bound to a read operation. Replace both handles with your configured values. The response body comes from that upstream; there is no universal AGINDOW success JSON wrapper.

example.code:
curl -i http://SIDECAR_HOST:8789/v1/guard \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"tool":"vendor.read","connection":"conn_example","operation":"read","args":{},"mode":"observe"}'

sections.heading: Successful or passed-through response
sections.text: The upstream HTTP status, content type and original body are returned when no policy halt applies. A vendor 4xx or 5xx can therefore be a completed upstream outcome. Inspect X-Agindow-Status separately from HTTP status. This illustrative 200 body belongs to a fictional upstream, not a fixed AGINDOW response schema.

example.code: {"id":"example-record","amount":2000}

sections.heading: Diagnostic headers
sections.text: Headers describe this call, not a protection guarantee. They may be absent when the host rejects a request before execution. Do not require numeric latency when the clock is unavailable.

rows: ok, repaired, degraded, bypassed or blocked. Current execution hosts do not apply selective repair.
Resolved observe, repair or strict policy when supplied.
Artifact ID, not a URL or promise of durable retention.
shape, semantic or unknown; present when drift evidence is available.
request, response or both; identifies which inspection phase found drift.
Active guard overhead excluding upstream waits; numeric locally or unavailable.
Clock source used by the remote execution host; may be unavailable.
Relative retained-outcome URL on a completed response halt. Read it; do not blindly replay a write.
Original upstream status on a local sidecar response halt.
When emitted by an authenticated remote host: allowance, remaining count and reset Unix seconds.
isolate when emitted; limits are local to an execution instance, not a global quota guarantee.

sections.heading: Policy refusal: HTTP 409
sections.text: An AGINDOW policy refusal has X-Agindow-Status: blocked and exactly six string fields below. repair uses drift_blocked; strict uses drift_halted. Observe never produces a policy block. A request halt means no dispatch. A response halt means the upstream already completed; inspect the retained outcome. An upstream 409 alone does not establish an AGINDOW policy refusal.

example.code:
{
  "error": "drift_blocked",
  "tool": "vendor.write",
  "drift_class": "semantic",
  "drift_id": "aud_example",
  "hint": "Upstream completed. Inspect the retained outcome; do not blindly replay a write.",
  "audit": "/v1/audit/aud_example"
}

sections.heading: Request validation, capacity and transport errors
sections.text: When the guard rejects a request before execution, it generally uses {"error":"code"}; framework limits or origin refusals may have a plain or empty body. Upstream bodies use the vendor format. Do not assume every non-2xx response is JSON or safe to retry.

rows: Malformed JSON, unknown field, invalid/mismatched route operation, missing idempotency key or unsupported durability.
Connection/tool not admitted locally, or remote credential missing/invalid.
Check the handles and credential; do not switch tenants to retry.

Check the path; a missing receipt does not prove non-execution.

Inspect feedback and retained outcome; do not blindly replay.
Envelope exceeds 8 MiB + 64 KiB, or arguments exceed the inspection bound.
Reduce the request; do not silently split a logical write.
This remote execution instance has reached its request limit.
Wait for the indicated reset if present; preserve the same logical idempotency key.
Sidecar could not obtain/read an upstream response.
Outcome may be uncertain. Reconcile writes before retrying.
Use an explicit SDK fallback if configured, with the same upstream-enforced key for writes.

sections.heading: Limits and retry safety
sections.text: The statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect. Configure detection separately; selecting a mode is insufficient. Response inspection requires a complete body within the configured size limit; streams, encoded or incomplete evidence can bypass inspection. A malformed whole body is not repaired. The local vendor timeout is 30 seconds. Client timeouts do not cancel an already completed vendor write. SDK remote helpers default to five seconds and require a caller-supplied fallback. Audit and outcome records have fixed retention limits and do not provide durable replay.

sections.heading: Versioned evidence record
sections.text: The complete JSON Schema below defines the audit response returned by the execution and MCP evidence APIs. Required nullable drift and patch fields distinguish absent evidence from a missing field. proof.write_integrity is an evidence claim, not a consequence of HTTP success; false means write integrity has not been established. Credential values do not belong in metadata.

sections.heading: Read a record
sections.text: id and ts identify the call; operation and mode identify its frozen policy; drift describes classification, side and optional changes; decision names the call outcome. patch is null when nothing changed, otherwise applied and byte_identical describe the patch. proof records contract_version, verified_against and write_integrity, plus an optional idempotency_key. confidence, hypothesis, detail, note and metadata are optional. Missing retained evidence is unavailable, not proof of a clean call.

sections.heading: Choose the same execution host
sections.text: These are sidecar/execution API routes, separate from MCP fetch_audit. Read them from the host that handled the call. Local socket access provides local authority; remote archive reads require the same credential used for execution and current authorization. Never follow an outcome URL to a different origin with credentials.

sections.heading: GET /healthz
sections.text: No body required. Sidecar response: {"status":"ok","instance":"example","registered":true,"calls":0}. This reports process health and a local call counter, not detector readiness, upstream health or write safety. An authenticated remote execution host may return only status and the default engine name.

sections.heading: GET /v1/registration
sections.text: Sidecar only. No request body. Returns instance (string), routes (an array such as ["conn_example/vendor.read"]) and default_engine (string). The statistical guest is default; configure windows to detect. Lists configured local connection/tool handles; it neither registers a workload nor grants authority. Do not expose a loopback sidecar as a public credential service.

sections.heading: GET /v1/audit/{id}
sections.text: Use the ID from X-Agindow-Audit or the audit URL in policy feedback. Returns an application/json audit artifact when retained: id, ts, tool, operation, mode, drift, decision, patch and proof, with optional confidence and metadata. See the schema reference for the full versioned shape. Not every streaming or bypass call has a retrievable artifact.

sections.heading: GET /v1/outcome/{id}
sections.text: Use X-Agindow-Outcome after a response halt. Returns the retained original upstream status, headers and body with X-Agindow-Retained-Outcome: true. The HTTP status can be an upstream error. Retrieval does not execute the operation again. A request halt has no completed upstream outcome.

example.code: curl -i http://SIDECAR_HOST:8789/v1/outcome/aud_example

sections.heading: Missing or unavailable evidence
sections.text: 404 means missing, expired, evicted, not captured, wrong host, or inaccessible evidence; it is not proof that a write never happened. The sidecar may return 503 internal when archive access fails. An unauthenticated remote read can return 401; remote credential mismatch or lost authorization is concealed as 404. Error bodies can be plain text. Retention is process-local: sidecar FIFO up to 128 entries / 16 MiB; remote host up to 64 entries / 16 MiB. Restarts and instance changes lose access. Reconcile uncertain writes with the vendor using the original idempotency key.

sections.heading: Exchange an existing workload identity
sections.text: Optional authenticated execution-host interface for integrations that already have an admitted workload identity. This is not public signup or dashboard login. Use the endpoint and registration supplied by your host owner; no managed token endpoint is issued. Send application/json; maximum body 32 KiB. Tokens expire and are sender-bound; refresh outside tool execution.

sections.heading: Request fields
sections.text: Unknown fields are rejected. JWT exchange uses a trusted workload assertion. Delegation uses an existing access token and cannot expand its authority.

rows: Workload assertion or parent access token. Never log it.
Existing admitted workload registration. Does not create one.
Intended execution audience; must match admitted authority.
Requested admitted tool names; delegation can only narrow scope.
Positive lifetime, at most 900 seconds and no longer than the source credential permits.

sections.text: Illustrative JWT exchange body. Replace the assertion, registration, audience and thumbprint with values admitted by your execution host; never paste real token material into prompts or logs.

sections.heading: Success: HTTP 200
sections.text: The response is application/json with Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache. access_token is sensitive; token_type is DPoP for jkt binding or Bearer for certificate binding. expires_at is Unix seconds. Use the corresponding proof or certificate on execution and recovery requests.

  "access_token": "<access-token>",
  "token_type": "DPoP",
  "issued_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token",
  "expires_in": 300,

sections.heading: Errors and retry behavior
sections.text: JSON errors use {"error":"code"}. 400 invalid_request or unsupported_grant_type: fix the request. 413: reduce body size. 401 identity_*: assertion, expiry or proof refused; acquire a valid identity rather than retry the same proof. 403 identity_*: scope, tenant or registration refused; ask the host owner to authorize this workload and scope. 429 identity_*: exchange capacity/rate exhausted; back off. 503 identity_unavailable or identity_*: exchange unavailable; refresh credentials outside the call path. Do not fall back to an unrelated credential automatically. Replay and rate state are local to one process, not shared across hosts.

Managed MCP access is not available.

sections.heading: Local interface preview
sections.text: Dependabot for agents. At runtime. Detect API drift as agents run, apply reviewed and verified runtime repairs, and turn drift evidence into validated source fixes and draft pull requests. Pre-alpha. Detection requires configured windows. Runtime repair is opt-in for supported changes. Source-fix tooling is available locally; hosted PR automation is not yet qualified. The signed tools contain the input and output schemas served by MCP. Never trust a public key merely because the response includes it.

sections.heading: Initialize
sections.text: `createAgindow` creates an SDK instance. Start in observe mode to keep original payloads and outcomes. Await `sdk.ready` before guarded calls: it resolves after the loading attempt, including a failed attempt. Loading/inspection failures surface as `bypass` events when a call runs. Readiness does not prove detection is configured; the default selection is empty.

sections.heading: Guard an existing API call
sections.text: Use Node 22.6+ for the native TypeScript run command (the SDK itself supports Node 22+). Save this complete example as `orders.mts`. Set `API_URL` to an existing HTTPS JSON order endpoint and run `node --experimental-strip-types orders.mts`. If it needs authentication, preserve the headers and credential handling in your existing HTTP client. Replace the function inside `sdk.guard` with that client call. The guarded function returns the original API value; it does not add an outcome wrapper. Label writes as `operation: write`. This example makes one read and has no detector selection, so a successful call normally prints an empty event list.

sections.heading: Inspect events
sections.text: `sdk.on(kind, listener)` subscribes to one event kind and returns an unsubscribe callback. Register listeners before running guarded calls. `sdk.recent()` returns the bounded local history, with a default capacity of 100. No event is emitted merely because a call succeeded; an empty list does not prove that an API is drift-free. These records are not a durable audit archive.

sections.heading: Configure detection
sections.text: Supply `selection` to `createAgindow` at construction. Its scope identifies tenant, connection, vendor, operation and segment; `selection.operation` must match the guarded tool, such as `orders.get`. Each selected field supplies request/response `side`, JSON Pointer `path`, complete baseline and current `live` JSON documents, and an `enumeration` setting. Use independent comparable windows from that operation. There is no automatic baseline learning. Missing or insufficient evidence can produce no finding; bypass is a different outcome. The complete executable guide keeps window construction out of this integration example.

sections.heading: Enable verified repair
sections.text: Selective repair is disabled by default. The local example below models a reviewed CRM top-level rename. Its verifier compares both payloads with an independently loaded application snapshot; a schema or matching values alone cannot establish migration intent. Replace the reviewed facts and local callable with your application-specific evidence and client. Begin in observe, evaluate the rule, then permit application with repair mode. `selectiveRepair` requires scoped rules, confidence and a synchronous `verify` callback; perform no network, database or LLM work inside it. Repair requires confidence at least 0.97, strict at least 0.99, complete supported captures and independent acceptance. These thresholds do not measure real-world accuracy. A `repair` event confirms application; a finding or proposed patch does not. Runtime payload repair does not modify repository source or create a pull request.

sections.text: Use per-call options and `sdk.configure` for future-call policy. `sdk.simulate` evaluates recordings without contacting an API. `sdk.drainAudit` is an explicit off-path Node-only delivery seam and requires audit configuration; it cannot be combined with selectiveRepair. import json
from agindow import Agindow, RenameRule, RepairCheck, SelectiveRepair
# Reviewed application snapshot, loaded independently before the call.
names = {"customer-123": "Ada"}
def verify(check: RepairCheck) -> bool:
    before = json.loads(check.before)
    after = json.loads(check.after)
    return bool(check.rule.migration == "crm-name-v2-reviewed"
                and after.get("id") in names and before.get("id") == after.get("id")
                and before.get("contact_name") == names[after["id"]]
                and after.get("display_name") == names[after["id"]])
sdk = Agindow(mode="observe", selective_repair=SelectiveRepair(
    rules=(RenameRule(tool="crm.customer", side="response", source="contact_name",
                      target="display_name", migration="crm-name-v2-reviewed", confidence=1.0),),
    verify=verify))
# Local illustration of a reviewed migration, not a vendor request.
@sdk.guard(tool="crm.customer", operation="read")
def customer() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"id": "customer-123", "contact_name": "Ada"}
try:
    sdk.configure(mode="repair")  # After evaluating the rule in observe.
    print(customer())
    print([event for event in sdk.recent() if event.type == "repair"])
finally:
    sdk.close()

sections.heading: Initialize
sections.text: `Agindow` loads during construction. `sdk.ready` is a boolean, not an awaitable. If loading fails, it is false and `sdk.load_error` retains the exception; guarded calls preserve the original outcome through bypass. Start in observe mode. A true ready value means the engine loaded, not that drift detection has been selected. Call `sdk.close()` when the instance is no longer needed.

sections.heading: Guard an existing API call
sections.text: Save this complete example as `orders.py`, set `API_URL` to your HTTPS JSON order endpoint, then run `python orders.py`. The `@sdk.guard` decorator wraps the existing Python function. Keep vendor authentication, request headers and timeouts in that function or your current client. The function remains synchronous and returns its ordinary API result; observe does not mutate it or enforce policy blocks. Use `operation="write"` for writes. This unconfigured example has no selected evidence windows, so an empty event list is expected after a successful read.

sections.heading: Guard an async operation
sections.text: Save as `orders_async.py` and run `python orders_async.py` with the same API_URL. Decorate an `async def` and await the guarded function normally. This standard-library example puts blocking HTTP work in `asyncio.to_thread`; use your existing async client directly when you have one. Original exceptions and cancellation propagate. Cancelling an await does not prove that a blocking thread or a vendor operation stopped. The SDK supplies a callable boundary, not a Python framework adapter.

sections.heading: Inspect events
sections.text: `sdk.on(kind, listener)` returns an unsubscribe callable; register before guarded calls. `sdk.recent()` returns a tuple of local events with a default capacity of 100. A `drift` event reports configured findings; `repair` means an accepted payload change was applied; `blocked` reports a policy halt; `bypass` reports unavailable or skipped inspection; `error` is diagnostic metadata. No success event is emitted. An empty tuple does not prove that an API is drift-free. Local history is not a durable audit archive. Python fields use names such as `event.drift_class` and `event.latency_us`.

sections.heading: Configure detection
sections.text: Construct `Agindow(selection=selection, mode="observe")` with a JSON-compatible dictionary. Scope it by tenant, connection, vendor, operation and segment; `operation` in the selection must match the tool, such as orders.get. Each field specifies request/response side, a JSON Pointer, complete raw JSON documents in baseline/live windows, and enumeration. Collect representative independent evidence for the same operation. The SDK does not learn baselines automatically. Missing or insufficient evidence can produce no finding. Python Verdict uses `drift_class` and does not expose the Node detector-name arrays. Follow the full runnable Python example before interpreting findings.

sections.heading: Enable verified repair
sections.text: Selective repair is opt-in. Use `SelectiveRepair`, `RenameRule` and a `RepairCheck` verifier through `selective_repair`. Python rule fields are source/target. The runnable local example below models a reviewed CRM response rename and checks an independent application snapshot. Replace its reviewed facts and callable for your own integration. A schema check or matching field values alone cannot establish intended meaning. Keep the verifier synchronous and local; load authoritative evidence before the call. Evaluate in observe, then use `sdk.configure(mode="repair")` to permit application. Confidence must reach 0.97 (0.99 in strict), and supported capture, policy and verification gates must accept. These thresholds are not measured accuracy. A repair event means an actual patch was applied. Runtime payload repair does not edit source files or open PRs.

sections.heading: Scopes, configuration and cleanup
sections.text: `sdk.wrap(fn, ...)` is the callable alternative to a decorator. Use `with sdk.context(mode="observe"):` or `async with sdk.context(mode="observe"):` for scoped overrides. ContextVar state belongs to this SDK and the current task; executing calls retain their snapshot. `sdk.configure(**changes)` changes future calls, while decorator keyword options can override instance/context settings. Close the instance in a finally block; later guarded calls bypass. The reference retains small sync/async scope examples and complete signatures.

sections.heading: Advanced boundaries
sections.text: `guard_remote` and `guard_remote_async` explicitly call a configured remote HTTP host; setting endpoint metadata does not move local calls to a service. No managed execution host is supplied. Python has no Node simulation method, HTTP/framework adapters, report CLI or guest audit drain. Pydantic-preserving projections and sync/async cancellation containment are local host behavior, not a guarantee of all framework or streaming coverage. A response-phase halt can follow a completed upstream write and cannot undo it. Both SDKs package the same detection engine; their language APIs remain different.

import asyncio
import json
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from threading import Thread
from agindow import (RemoteEnvelope, RemoteOptions, RemoteResponse,
                     guard_remote, guard_remote_async)

original_calls = 0
# Original application read; replace with your existing client in an integration.
def read_customer(input: RemoteEnvelope) -> RemoteResponse:
    global original_calls
    original_calls += 1
    body = json.dumps({"id": "customer-123", "name": "Ada"}).encode()
    return RemoteResponse(200, {"content-type": "application/json"}, body)

# Protocol fixture only: fixed read binding, no engine or vendor call.
class Host(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self) -> None:
        value = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
        if (self.path != "/v1/guard" or value["tool"] != "crm.read"
                or value["connection"] != "local" or value["operation"] != "read"):
            self.send_error(400)
            return
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"id": value["args"]["id"], "name": "Ada"}).encode())
    def log_message(self, format: str, *args: object) -> None:
        pass

host = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Host)
thread = Thread(target=host.serve_forever, daemon=True)
thread.start()
envelope = RemoteEnvelope(tool="crm.read", connection="local", operation="read",
                          args={"id": "customer-123"}, mode="observe")
options = RemoteOptions(endpoint=f"http://127.0.0.1:{host.server_port}/v1/guard",
                        timeout_seconds=1)
def show(result: RemoteResponse) -> None:
    try:
        customer = json.loads(result.read())
        assert result.status == 200 and customer["id"] == "customer-123"
        print(result.status, customer)
    finally:
        result.close()
async def main() -> None:
    # Async helper takes the same synchronous fallback, running in a worker thread.
    show(await guard_remote_async(read_customer, envelope, options))
try:
    show(guard_remote(read_customer, envelope, options))
    asyncio.run(main())
    assert original_calls == 0
finally:
    host.shutdown()
    host.server_close()
    thread.join()
# Closed endpoint: original read supplies this call's value.
show(guard_remote(read_customer, envelope, options))
assert original_calls == 1

Choose remote execution when your application intentionally delegates a configured tool call to a separate HTTP guard host. You supply and operate that endpoint and its connection bindings; managed execution is not available. Use embedded execution to inspect your existing callable inside the application. Setting endpoint or apiKey on an embedded SDK never changes its transport.

sections.heading: Authentication and security
sections.text: Basic endpoint authentication: explicitly pass apiKey (Node) or api_key (Python) in RemoteOptions only when the host admits that legacy credential. It sends Authorization: Bearer and emits legacy_unbound through the diagnostic callback. Obtain credentials from your host operator and secret storage; public key issuance is unavailable. Embedded Config credentials are not automatically copied into remote options. Use HTTPS for non-loopback endpoints and keep vendor secrets in host connection bindings. The local fixture intentionally needs no credential. These option-builder snippets expect your host-issued credential as an argument; they do not acquire credentials or make a call.

sections.heading: Prepare sender-bound credentials
sections.text: When your host supports workload identity, prefer an explicitly acquired auth session. Node createProofSigner() returns thumbprint and proof(token, method, target, now). await createRemoteAuth({acquire, signer?, schedule?}) calls your acquire(thumbprint) outside guarded calls; it must exchange against your trusted identity service and return {accessToken, expiresAt} in Unix seconds. Pass {endpoint, auth} to guardRemote and close the session at shutdown. Python RemoteAuth(acquire, signer, schedule=True) requires a host-owned ProofSigner(public_x, sign); acquire(thumbprint) returns AccessCredential(access_token, expires_at). Its refresh() is synchronous and returns bool; close() stops background refresh. workload_identity prepares the explicit platform identity source. Both languages require trusted exchange setup; no signer or credentials are discovered from the envelope. headers(method, target) never acquires identity inside a call; refresh runs separately. Expired/unavailable proof material invokes fallback, while an endpoint 401/403 remains a response. Do not pass both auth and apiKey/api_key. Legacy fallback requires explicit auth-session opt-in; it is never automatic discovery.

sections.heading: Install and run
sections.text: Inspect supported integration definitions and generate offline reports without executing your application. The CLI ships with the Node SDK, not as a separate Python tool. Use Node 22+ and install the selected version with `npm install agindow@0.1.0-alpha.3`. The installed binary is `agindow`; from that project directory run the command below. `.` means the current directory. Report reads supported JS/TS source recursively, but does not import/execute the project, write project files or contact providers. Installation itself may use the network.

sections.heading: Generate your first report
sections.text:
1. Open your supported JS/TS project. For a reproducible exercise, use a clean directory and save the fixture below as tools.ts; it need not be executed or have LangChain installed.
2. Run npx --no-install agindow report . after installing the CLI there.
3. Read the text on stdout. There is no default report file. To save it yourself, use npx --no-install agindow report . > agindow-report.txt. Shell redirection writes that file.
4. Review discovered tools and skipped files, then collect scoped runtime evidence before drawing conclusions about drift.
